The ground noise model is typically omitted from channel formulations for single-antenna multiple-access systems because it can be incorporated seamlessly by adjusting the channel matrix. Its influence becomes integral when considering multi-antenna models for point-to-point communications. By isolating ground noise within a two-antner setup, researchers found that it reduces the capacity of the non-antial systems. This finding underscores the necessity of accounting for ground noise in the design and analysis of wireless networks, particularly within terrestrial environments where its impact is non-negligible.

While standard quantum optics experiments typically demonstrate Bell nonlocality only via violations of Bell inequalities, flawless examples of Bell nonlocality without inequalities can also be observed in correlations arising from continuously variable (CV) entangled states, typically requiring Gaussian noise and detection schemes. Specifically, when single-photon detectors are employed, the necessary conditions to violate Bell inequalities are very stringent; however, these conditions are significantly relaxed for matching ideal correlations with the derived non-inegalitarian proof using non-Gaussian operations on CV entangled states. Furthermore, under realistic scenarios involving detector inefficiency and miscellaneous losses, it remains possible to flawlessly establish both types of Bell nonlocality if the initial state features higher photon numbers after subtraction.

This study examines how an electron interacts with an optical lattice modulated at its roton frequency under two distinct types of modulation—squared amplitude versus random phase—and investigates the resulting changes in DC conductivity at both the band level and experimental level. Specifically, amplitude-squared modulation suppresses conductivity by an order of magnitude compared to random phase modulation. These findings are grounded in a tight-binding model where we analyze model parameters at the band level to revise the traditionally accepted "level bands" concept for optical lattice systems. Our revised framework suggests a critical role for the conduction band width in determining conductivity magnitude. We further support this theoretical analysis with simulations based on a convectional Bose-Hubbard model.

Superconducting activity in a new hydride material, LaH$_{9}$, was famously reported at a record-breaking pressure of 190 GPa. This remarkable achievement prompted scientists to investigate other hydrogen-rich compounds in their quest for superconducting states that function at lower pressures. Recently, solid solutions incorporating hydrogen and boron have gained significant attention, as both elements individually form E$_{g}$-type molecules with three-membered rings when embedded within alkaline earth lattices, offering the potential to stabilize such structures through coexistence. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive examination of hydrogen boron-based materials using first-principles methods. We report the synthesis of a newly discovered C2/m phase for LaH$_{3}$B, featuring a 24-atom molecular framework, which exhibits a phonon spectrum free of instabilities. Furthermore, we analyze the phonon-driven electron-phonon interactions across various hydrogen boron systems. Our calculations reveal that these interactions remain relatively weak, with a maximum coupling constant ($\lambda$) of 0.85 for the C2/m phase of EuH$_{3}$B, leading to an estimated but modest superconducting critical temperature ($T_{c}$) of 22 K. Collectively, our findings offer initial insights but indicate that strong superconducting effects arise only from subtle engineering effects in these systems.

In shared-memory multiprocessors, cache pollution caused by cross-process memory accesses remains a primary performance bottleneck. To address this, researchers have developed dynamic run allocation techniques that identify polluting accesses and partition addresses spaces to minimize them. However, these methods suffer from inefficiency due to the frequent migration of processes between partitions. We introduce novel pollution metrics that flatten address spaces into single logical partitions, thereby eliminating partition boundaries and reducing the complexity of the partitioning state. We also propose two algorithms, RURA and IRURA, which utilize these new metrics to distribute runs across this flattened structure. RURA operates via simple greedy selection to choose a home partition for each process, whereas IRURA employs an iterative refinement phase to progressively enhance performance. Evaluation against both simulated shared-memory multiprocessors and real system traces demonstrates that run distribution based on our proposed polling measures outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, these run allocation experiments yield significant performance gains over baseline systems that lack such optimization.

Existing clustering methods for dynamical systems primarily rely on distance metrics derived from state space or flow properties. In this paper, we propose an innovative data-driven approach that estimates an influence value between dynamical systems. The proposed method offers distinct advantages: it is fully offline and does not require access to underlying dynamical system models. Furthermore, we prove that this approach satisfies the triangle inequality, and we show that in practice this metric scales better than traditional distance measures.

To address these issues, this paper proposes AGCN, a novel adaptive graph convolutional model designed specifically for forecasting multi-dimensional time series. Unlike prior static-generative models, which assign a single fixed graph to all data, AGCN learns a continuous graph topology from the input data space that changes dynamically based on the temporal context. Furthermore, to enhance interpretability, this work introduces a method for time-varying node importance estimation by analyzing the adaptive node weights within this continuous framework. Experimental evaluations across diverse real-world datasets confirm that AGCN significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art forecasting methods.

Although recent searches have yielded no results, there is still room for low-mass electrically neutral particles to couple with protons and neutrons, given that their associated effects within nuclear media are heavily obscured by intrinsic nuclear complexity. Identifying human actions in video remains a difficult computer vision challenge, particularly when relying on conventional 2D frame analysis, which results in critical motion context loss. To address this and enhance feature extraction from sequential frames, we introduce a novel architectural solution termed the Hierarchical Focus Network (HFN) for action recognition. HFN integrates two core mechanisms designed to capture temporal dependencies: the Temporal Focus Network (TFN) and the R-Optical Flow Network (OFN). The OFN module generates an adaptive motion map by learning from redundant optical flow data within sliding windows, effectively reducing redundancy. Simultaneously, the TFN module sequences these maps using long short-term memory (LSTM) units to establish temporal connections. Furthermore, to ensure the model's efficiency, both components are implemented on multiple levels to progressively refine the information. We evaluated the proposed HFN against state-of-the-art methods on two major benchmarks, MIT Action Recognition 10 (10-15-15) and UT-Action 10 (10-15-15-15-15), achieving superior performance.

Monitoring biological motion in video is vital for detecting threats, identifying individuals, and counting people in security applications. This study investigates how electrons couple with phonons in two-dimensional (material) systems that exhibit unique interaction mechanisms, specifically those involving charge carriers confined to curved trajectories within a two-dimensional plane. Such systems, theoretically predicted to exist within few-layer MoS₂ under strong magnetic fields, are characterized by valley-specific electron-phonon coupling arising from distinct phonon coupling constants and modified carrier dynamics. Our findings reveal two novel mechanisms: a phonon-induced shift in valley (distinct) energy levels and a phonon-mediated alteration in carrier mobility, both of which are highly sensitive to temperature. These hallmarks—valley-dependent energy level shifts in valleytronics and temperature-sensitive mobility changes—are expected to enable new technologies utilizing valley control through acoustic or thermal manipulation. These findings offer critical insights into valley-based electronics and enable fresh experimental tests to validate valley control via phonons.

This paper introduces a cloud, defined as a compact subset of the compact clouded set (CCTS) that possesses the property of being arbitrarily close to the shape of some complete metric space with diameter no larger than a specified value delta. We demonstrate that every cloud satisfies several key characteristics: it remains within delta proximity to a unique metric space called its hub, and the mapping cloud-to-hub induces an isometry upon identifying maximally periodic functions among continuous bounded maps to any given metric space. Additionally, the paper proves that a metric space is compact if and only if it satisfies the condition that for each potential distance threshold, there exists a collection of clouds equidistant to it within that tolerance whose union is also compact. Finally, the authors show that a set qualifies as a cloud precisely when it can be represented as the uniform convergence limit of a sequence of clouds from increasingly smaller diameter constraints.

This paper presents the design, analysis, and experimental validation of miniaturized millimeter-wave patch antennas featuring wide bandwidth and an extensive spatial coverage. Operating within the IEEE 802.15.3a standard, this protocol supports millimeter-wave frequencies from 60 to 92.5 GHz, yet has seen limited adoption in recent antenna research. The antennas are configured for both transmission and reception, utilizing surface-relief etched (SRE) dielectric lenses to achieve compact dimensions and high directivity. The architecture employs an array of four radiating elements, each equipped with cross-shaped slots to enhance impedance matching and broaden operational frequencies. A feeding mechanism, designed with a transmission line and integrated stubs, improves isolation between adjacent wide elements. Measurements across 60 to 92.5 GHz reveal an impedance return loss better than -15 dB and an out-of-tilt gain exceeding 10.5 dBi. The antennas exhibit stable radiation patterns with low cross-polarization levels, maintaining consistent gain and half-power beamwidth values. Additionally, measurements of the specific array configuration show consistent axial and half-power beamwidth characteristics. Ultimately, this work offers a novel, highly performant antenna architecture suited for the IEEE 802.15.3a specification.

Furthermore, empirical analysis of the model's long-term behavior demonstrates effective calibration capabilities using real-world market data.

Short baseline neutrino experiments have recently established their feasibility in seeking oscillations driven by sterile states. Although current limits preclude discussing specific probabilities, the upcoming Long-Baseline Neutrino facility (DUNE) offers a promising avenue to probe these short baselines simultaneously. This analysis examines DUNE's sensitivity to e- and ν-type sterile states and identifies optimal long-distance run configurations to maximize sensitivity while integrating the primary long-distance mission. Using 6.6 proton beam years of data, we can exclude sterile states with mass squared differences up to approximately 14.44 eV. For e- neutrino oscillations, this corresponds to resonances below 14.44 eV. However, to probe deeper, we can extend the run distance to around 540.4 meters, effectively excluding resonances up to 14.44 eV. In summary, we can exclude sterile states with mass squared differences up to approximately 14.44 eV.

Meta-analysts often struggle to obtain reliable estimates when dealing with multiple correlated effect sizes from the same research study. Although recent cluster-aware methodological strategies exist, they fail to account for the potential nonlinearity inherent in logarithmic random-effects model transformations. This study introduces two novel cluster-robust variance estimation methods specifically tailored for random-effect models and evaluates their performance against standard approaches. Simulations are conducted for a bivariat context and combined with multilevel structures to test the new methods and compare them using available options. The new methods are available in R through the package robustmetaef.

Particle-resolved simulations are commonly used to analyze fluid-particle interactions at the mesoscale, considering individual shapes, sizes, and fluid properties. However, resolving the non-instantaneous, finite-duration collision between a particle and a wall or another particle requires time-integration methods capable of bridging multiple time-scales. This study proposes such a method, where the local time-step is dynamically adjusted based on the physical duration of a collision. By integrating equations of motion with acceleration terms derived from multiple contact models, the initial fast approach phase and subsequent equilibrium phase are simulated smoothly. Results from a particle-fluid system with elastic collisions demonstrate that this algorithm accurately captures collision kinetics and hydrodynamic forces, despite employing time-steps varying by three orders of magnitude. Further tests on orthogonal collisions and sedimentation confirm the correctness of the angular momentum balance and mass conservation. Consequently, the introduced multi-timescale integration scheme facilitates the physical simulation of the full process, from particle fluidization through to deformation during impact.

An energy-emitting process, governed by a conservation of energy principle, compellingly seeks to identify its energy origin. The present study examines this inquiry within the framework of the Unruh effect and black hole radiation. It concludes that in both scenarios, the emission's source resides outside the realm of physical validity, thereby asserting that these phenomena cease to occur under conditions adhering to fundamental physical laws.

The color dipole method stands as a widely utilized framework for calculating particle production in high-energy hadronic collisions. In this approach, particle creation is modeled as the interaction between color dipoles from opposing protons, where each proton is viewed as a collection of dipoles proceeding toward the center-of-mass frame. Because of this constituent composition, the system inherently possesses a net lateral momentum imbalance, generating an asymmetric particle flow relative to the center-of-mass region. This work quantifies the resulting lateral momentum asymmetry within particle production using the color dipole method at LHC energies. Lateral momentum asymmetry is defined as the ratio of two rapidity distributions shifted along the rapidity axis so that their maximum values align at zero. The calculation of this metric confirms the presence of such an imbalance resulting from nuclear lateral momentum asymmetry. Specifically, the color dipole method predicts a maximum of the rapid distribution to be approximately 1.5 instead of the expected unity. Additionally, the lateral momentum asymmetry exhibits a non-zero value extending over a range of up to several units in rapidity. These findings suggest that experiments at the LHC can empirically verify this predicted momentum imbalance, thereby offering a test of the validity inherent to the color dipole method.

Assuming small amplitude parameters, the governing equations were formulated using the long-wave approximation, subsequently analyzed via the parametric variational method to determine the emergent instabilities. As a widely adopted feature in contemporary computing, Non-Volatile Memory (NVM) enables direct persistent storage within system memory, allowing processors immediate access to data without the latency of traditional external storage interfaces. This capability is particularly valuable in High-Performance Computing (HPC) environments, where transferring massive datasets across system boundaries creates significant performance bottlenecks. NVM presents an alternative to moving data, yet ensuring data resilience against power failures remains a critical hurdle. Current strategies typically employ dedicated algorithms to preserve consistency by writing only essential metadata to NVM, a method constrained by limited write endurance. Although checksums offer protection against memory corruption, they cannot prevent the inconsistency inherent in unstructured data writes. Addressing this gap, this paper introduces PG-CR—a crash-recovery algorithm specifically engineered for unstructured persistent in-memory stores. PG-CR operates by maintaining system state within log-organized pages, writing full page images to NVM, and utilizing a mechanism of live page replacement. Because replacing active pages consumes less endurance than appending individual records, this approach maximizes NVM write durability. Furthermore, since every replaced page represents complete context, every NVM image constitutes a self-contained execution unit, allowing the system to resume processing from the point of interruption following a crash. Evaluations demonstrate that this algorithm delivers performance comparable to, and in some cases exceeding, that of standard kernel mechanisms, while providing similar or better overall reliability.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in deriving network structures such as communities, cores, and layers for both information and social networks. However, the majority of existing methods for network restructuring have focused on small to medium-sized information networks. Consequently, the community is currently lacking in solutions capable of offering global structural insights into large-scale networks comprising millions of entities. This work presents the development of a unified framework that integrates both structural refinement and visualization techniques. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the proposed approach can be implemented using multiple algorithms offering varying degrees of scalability and resource efficiency. Finally, the study validates this integrated method through experiments on diverse real-world datasets ranging from thousands to hundreds of millions of nodes, and it compares the results against both proprietary and open-source software tools.

When contrasted with conventional forecasting methods, our statistical approach demonstrated superior accuracy. Furthermore, we conducted assessments of our approach's reliability by testing it on artificial datasets generated from known periodic and quasi-periodic configurations.

Furthermore, we have adapted this principal feature selection methodology for use with parallel computing architectures. Our adjusted algorithm leverages this parallelization to enhance overall test efficiency.

Subsequently, the study explores how the DSSN successfully models contextual logic in text and effectively leverages complementary data from multiple modalities to achieve highly precise classification.

Accurately representing multiphase flow interfaces is vital for both physical models and numerical simulations. However, achieving a mathematically concise description while maintaining sufficient interface resolution remains difficult. This study examines interface skeletons as a potential solution. Resolving long-standing issues, it demonstrates that these skeletons can be explicitly and unambiguously defined for standard interface representations used in computational fluid dynamics. The proposed explicit definition is valid for both level set and front-tracking methods while allowing for explicit interface tracking. The practical application of this concept is illustrated through various test cases, including but not limited to a rising bubble in two dimensions and a breaking wave in three dimensions.

Recent research has revealed that measles viruses can spontaneously roll across surfaces and even enter cells on their own. While the internal mechanics driving this movement remain unclear, this study demonstrates that a simple virion structure can generate self-directed rolling through the periodic conversion of chemical energy into motion. Our proposal features a rod-shaped virus model equipped with internal motors that push against spiral filaments, analogous to how left-handed microtubule motor proteins function in cells. We apply computational methods to outline the virus's overall movement trajectory and employ a simplified mathematical framework to analyze the system's one-dimensional dynamics, revealing bifurcation behavior inherent in this system. Energy analysis shows that approximately 0.1% of the total energy consumed by the virus is converted into actual movement. Finally, our proposed mechanical model aligns well with observed characteristics of rolling viruses seen in nature.

This mode suggests the existence of spontaneous broken symmetry at the macroscopic scale, characteristic of chirality within the vibrational spectrum. The Born effective charge is a pivotal concept in condensed matter physics, particularly for characterizing polar crystals. Traditionally defined in terms of a Born effective polarization, this definition assumes the adiabatic movement of an ion relative to other electrons and atoms. However, when significant non-adiabatic corrections arise, these mobility effects give rise to finite, non-perturbative contributions to ac electrical conductivity from periodic ion oscillations. We demonstrate that these contributions stem from both electronic and atomic degrees of freedom and are governed by quantities analogous to the Drude weight but featuring positive and negative charge carriers, respectively; notably, these Drude-like terms are finite even in the absence of band gap. Consequently, materials lacking a band gap—such as simple metals or plasmas—exhibit non-zero non-perturbative contributions to their AC conductivity. Conversely, if a system possesses a band gap, these non-adiabatic contributions vanish. Thus, the derived expression provides a fresh conceptual framework for understanding and potentially measuring the Drude weight and related physical effects.

This study investigates the effects of dissipation-level dissipativity on both rotating and non-rotating two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) turbulence. The analysis focuses on how changes in the large-scale flow structure, particularly when transitioning toward more dissipative regimes, influence turbulent characteristics. In non-rotating environments, increasing the dissipation scale causes the disturbance flow field to become increasingly irrotational; under sufficiently dissipative conditions, large vortices emerge. Within rotating systems, the response depends critically on the interaction between the Rossby radius of deformation and the dissipative scale. When transition to a highly dissipative state occurs, significant alterations occur in TKE (TKE stands for turbulent kinetic energy) and potential energy distributions, as well as a marked increase in disturbance heat flux. These findings underscore the critical role that large-scale flow organization plays in determining how turbulent energy and potential energy distributions behave.

The increasing availability of massive electronic health records has fueled numerous studies utilizing machine learning models for medication recommendation systems. These approaches typically define tasks such as recommending novel drugs or ranking medication pairs, often employing machine learning techniques like deep learning to capture complex interactions. However, the utility of these models is constrained by a lack of generalizability to new data due to insufficient understanding of intrinsic pharmacological mechanisms. In response, this study introduces "CoPhens," a cohesive model that integrates current pharmacological knowledge with deep learning to create a unified medication recommendation system. In addition to the system's generalization capabilities, evaluation metrics for each test set were analyzed to identify specific drug-drug pairs that enhance model performance beyond training data. Results indicate that CoPhens effectively identifies clinically significant paired medications, including combinations with documented adverse effects or novel pairings verified by external databases. In conclusion, this research demonstrates that explicitly embedding pharmacological mechanisms into the system enhances overall generalization and provides medical experts with interpretable insights into the rationale behind medication pair scores.

Identifying road hazards such as potholes is crucial for public safety. While automated detection offers a cost-effective solution, the current reliance on visual data processed by deep learning creates significant challenges for deploying systems across different countries. These limitations stem from inconsistent road conditions, varied camera types, diverse angles, and the lack of extensive, unbiased datasets representing multiple regions. To address this, we propose a novel dataset, MARS (Multi-Attribute Road Dataset), which aggregates 150,000 annotated harm images from eight distinct sources to promote fairness and breadth. Furthermore, we introduce PH2PL, a phase-based partial least regression model tailored for transfer learning that minimizes the need for massive pre-training datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses both the baseline MARS model and existing state-of-the-art techniques.

Imitation distribution shift is a critical challenge in the field of imprecision learning, yet current solutions predominantly concentrate on it within single-domain contexts. Real-world deployments, however, often involve scenarios where the expert domains and observation domains differ across regions. In such cross-domain settings, expert policies trained in one domain may transfer poorly to another due to distribution shift, particularly when domain-specific factors are embedded in the expert actions. Addressing this gap, we introduce Cross-Area Imitation from Observation (CAIO), a novel framework designed to mitigate domain-dependent biases. Instead of requiring action-level access to experts, CAIO employs a domain-invariant latent variable encoder paired with a domain-expert policy maker to capture the fundamental skill underlying expert behavior. By extracting this domain-independent representation, effective policy learning becomes achievable despite discrepancies between domains. Extensive evaluations across diverse real-world and simulated environments validate both the significance of cross-domain set-ups and the superior performance of the CAIO approach, particularly in contexts limited by the unavailability of direct action-level expert information.

A disk forming around a Population III protostar is subject to an exponentially growing ambient magnetic field, which fundamentally alters its physical behavior. Even at low values, this field generates an extremely strong magnetic pressure that dramatically swells magnetic loop sizes; if oriented radially, these loops can extend beyond the disk's radius. We analyze a vertically isothermal, locally isodense system where the Rossby number is much less than one, and we find that the classic magnetorotational instability (MRI) no longer applies. Instead, a new instability emerges that drives both strong vertical magnetic stretching and significant mass accretion, driven by the interaction between rotation and gravity rather than pure rotational shear. When this modified instability operates in a magnetized disk with low external field strength, vertical loop expansion induces intense amplification of the field, triggering a self-reorganization into a predominantly radial field configuration. This phase transition boosts both the Rossby number and the magnetization level, creating a feedback loop that enhances magnetic effects exponentially. Ultimately, this runaway process generates powerful outward magnetic forces that counteract gravitational collapse, effectively suppressing the fragmentation of the disk into a second star—a critical finding for understanding how the first single stars succeeded in avoiding dual accretion channels.

Association rule mining serves as a fundamental yet versatile technique across numerous data analysis domains. This paper introduces two frameworks to support this versatility: the deduction representation model and repetition representations. In an attempt to formalize deductive reasoning in association rule mining—as first proposed by Khanna et al. (2008)—we extend Khanna's initial model. Furthermore, we expand its scope by introducing the broader deducibility relationship. We demonstrate that the deducibility relationship retains all theoretically desirable properties anticipated for association rule mining applications.

Additionally, both deduction and repetition representations enable a unified approach to defining minimal bases for association rules. While both frameworks achieve this goal, they rely on distinct methods for assessing rule equivalence. We evaluate the interactions between these representations and their respective equivalence relations, focusing on issues related to computational complexity. Our analysis reveals that both representations are computationally sound regarding decidability and exist within polynomial time complexity classes.

This study examines how mandated mental health treatment influences recidivism within the criminal justice system. Using comprehensive data from North Carolina, which details inmate mental health screenings, initial charges, convictions, and program participation, the researchers analyzed outcomes across various offense types through logistic regression models. These models incorporated random effects associated with courts and screening results to control for unobserved heterogeneity, thereby enhancing the precision of estimates. Findings reveal that court-level mental health issues significantly lower recidivism rates for all offenses except violent crimes, whereas the impact of an individual's screened mental health condition varies by offense type. Specifically, person-level mental health matters significantly for property offenses but shows no significant effect on violent crime or drug offenses. By addressing court-level correlations, these enhanced models indicate that mental health conditions substantially reduce the risk of re-offending compared to earlier, less adjusted estimates. Finally, while treatment participation shows some statistical connection to reduced recidivism, courts with greater average treatment involvement do not necessarily exhibit lower repeat offense rates, suggesting that current models may underestimate the true efficacy of these programs.

This study introduces a parametric variant of the generalized Apostol–Bernoulli type $n$ polynomials alongside a corresponding series of identities. We further investigate and establish key properties regarding the parametric generalized Apostol–Bernoulli functions.

Dynamical spectrum access is increasingly recognized as a viable method to alleviate congestion in wireless communication. Multimodal biometric systems have gained significant traction as a secure method for secure access control due to the reliability offered by combining biometric traits. Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Machine Translation (MT) are resource-intensive areas that rely heavily on large, annotated datasets. Estimating the mean of a parametric distribution is a fundamental statistical task. This study examines the One-Sided Differential Privacy framework within database query contexts involving dependent variables. Our analysis reveals that while One-Sided Differential Privacy theoretically allows for the reduction of bound accuracy errors through adaptive strategies to near-zero levels in specific scenarios, practical implementation of such mechanisms results in information loss. This study investigates the anisotropic structure of heavy quark fragmentation by applying the general propagator framework within a finite external magnetic field. Previous research has demonstrated that early and strict lockdown measures during a pandemic effectively minimize both fatalities and economic losses. A graph $G$ is edge-tinted robustly if there exists a way to color its edges so that every vertex $v$ sees a uniform distribution of colors around it; specifically, for a graph with maximum degree $\Delta$ and $c$ colors, each $v$ exhibits exactly $\Delta/c$ edges of each color. When $\Delta$ is divisible by $c$, this uniform distribution implies that $G$ admits an equitable edge-partition divided into $c$ distinct parts (or equivalently, $G$ is equitably partible into $c$ independent sets). Historically, it was conjectured by Borodin et al. that all cubic bipartite graphs possess this robust edge tinting using three colors. However, in this note, we identify specific cubic bipartite graphs where the symmetry required for robustness is mathematically impossible, thereby providing concrete counterexamples.

A function $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ exhibits the convexity property on the Hamming graph if, for all adjacent vertices $x$ and $y$, the inequality $(f(x)-f(y))(f(x+u)-f(y+u)) \geq 0$ holds for any standard basis vector $u$; equivalently, each column of function values is ordered monotonically. This paper derives spectral conditions that guarantee such convexity. Specifically, we prove that if the Fourier coefficients of $f$ are nonnegative, $f$ is convex, or more broadly, if $f$'s Fourier coefficients are nonnegative (implying convexity), then the property holds. Additionally, by applying a sufficient condition for convexity to functions with arbitrary Fourier coefficients (positive semidefinite), we identify specific monotonic arrangements where convexity is assured. In one instance, this yields a bound of $f(i) \geq f(j)$ for all $i \leq j$, confirming convexity. Finally, our findings are utilized to re-establish a sufficient condition for log-concavity established by O. Tamuz.

COPASI, a versatile, cross-platform command, is used for performing computational modeling of biochemical pathways. Its extensive suite of analysis tools supports simulation of dynamics of pathways to steady-state analysis of steady-state of systems, stability analysis of steady-state of systems, sensitivity analysis of steady-state of systems, parameter estimation based on data, molecular distance computation and assembly of large molecular networks into smaller components called supermolecules. Although its capabilities are extensive, running simulations via command line can be challenging for users who lack experience with command line environments. Furthermore, manipulating data for these simulations often requires local storage and processing power. To overcome these limitations, our team developed ShinyCOPASI, which offers an intuitive graphical user interface accessible directly through a web browser. This tool allows researchers to upload local models and data files, configure experiments, execute simulations, and visualize outcomes without needing local computational resources or installing software.

In Science AI, ensuring model explainability is critical for trust and acceptance within the research community to facilitate the integration of AI into experimental design, data analysis, and the interpretation of results and protocols. While recent efforts have utilized global methods like machine table to provide a unified classification and comparison of explainability techniques for scientific algorithms—covering approaches from black-box interpretations to sensitive feature selection and probabilistic metrics—this work advances that framework by introducing Ambiguity Quantification as a novel evaluation criterion. Specifically addressed is data noise, or "ambiguity," regarding a model's sensitivity to perturbations in inputs relative to those inputs' actual quality; to formalize this, we propose a new metric based on the correlation between a model's output rank and the intrinsic value of training data, utilizing efforts aligned with our definition for measuring explainability model performance across datasets such as MNIST, CIFAR-10, Drosophila morphometrics, and others.

The paper analyzes this algebra in instances where it fails to be a type $U I$ von Neumann algebra. System identification involves determining a dynamical system's model from observed data, a process often complicated by uncertainty regarding the true system model. This uncertainty necessitates robust estimation techniques capable of yielding implied estimates bounded by data variability. This study introduces an adaptive impurity scheme for combining precision and system robustness under uncertain data conditions. The proposed method integrates robust bound estimation with an adaptive system robustness filter derived from implicate data analysis via iterative refinement using modified generalised Krylov subspace methods. Although generalised methods are typically viewed as requiring strict data consistency, the refination process effectively handles non-consistent datasets by adapting to variability. The effectiveness of this approach is verified through two-dimensional (2-D) system identification examples based on Markov decision processes.

Computer-generated time series data are frequently employed to model complex, time-dependent phenomena. In this paper, we address a novel inverse problem aimed at recovering a finite set of computer simulation contours that best fit observed time series values. This proposed approach is uniquely suited to scenarios where physical processes are too intricate to formulate explicitly, as it integrates a "black box" simulation directly into an optimization objective. By leveraging this embedding, we can estimate otherwise hard-to-characterize processes, thereby enhancing our ability to understand dynamic systems through targeted computational experimentation. The study presents an optimization framework tailored for this specific contour estimation task and introduces a specialized algorithm. This method employs sequential low-to-high resolution evaluations to maintain estimation precision while significantly cutting down the impact of numerical approximation errors. We validate the approach using synthetic time series populated by various continuous functions, as well as real-world functional datasets generated by the Lorenz-Stenflo system.

Recent studies have demonstrated that incorporating query regularization via region queries enhances model robustness against adversarial examples. However, the underlying mechanism explaining why regional queries regulate learning remains poorly understood. This work seeks to address that gap by examining how different query types influence the sensitivity of loss functions to specific regions in the input space. Our research investigates these queries within both non-adversarial and adversatorial settings, analyzing them through the lens of linear models and their adversarial performance. We validate our findings empirically using linear models and extend the analysis theoretically to adaptive threats within the framework of minimax-optimizable problems. Ultimately, we conclude that while effective in clean or weakly adversarial environments, region queries offer no advantage over no querying under strong adversarial conditions; our theoretical analysis identifies specific attributes of input distributions and region shapes that determine when their usage is beneficial.

In this study, we examine how jets fragment within the medium by analyzing the groomed fragmentation functions of these jets in events tagged with an isolated photon. This specific tag offers precise event-by-event constraints on the transverse momentum balance before the jet enters the medium. We observe that for a fixed pre-medium $p_{\text{T}}$ balance, the medium modifies the jet fragmentation function in a manner consistent with a collective softening effect. This conclusion is supported by comparing our data to simulations from the Monte Carlo model MC@NLO coupled with JETSET, which further confirms the data's sensitivity to such medium-induced alterations in jet fragmentation.

Noting that previous work on colored multiple zeta functions treats summation indices as non-negative integers, this note introduces sequences following the Apery model via multi-index indices with mixed parity. This framework enables new evaluations for various modified colored multiple zeta functions and extends our findings to new infinite dimensions.

On the night of June 29, 2019, the *Swift* X-ray telescope unexpectedly captured a bright flash from a young brown dwarf, an incident that has sparked considerable interest among researchers. This study presents the first comprehensive multi-wavelength analysis of the event, utilizing optical data from *Pan-STARRS1* and *TESS*, as well as near-infrared observations from *2MASS*, *VISTA*, and *WISE*. Our findings indicate that the optical and near-infrared signatures are best explained by a short-duration optical phenomenon, likely resulting from a minor surface collision involving a small object, with a duration of only about 19 minutes. Although the brown dwarf, known as WISEA J153429.75-104303.3, has not been previously observed to exhibit such optical variability, its behavior closely mirrors that of the field of young, rapidly rotating brown dwarfs, suggesting it belongs to a similar evolutionary group. Furthermore, the timing of this outburst aligns with a specific phase in the brown dwarf's rotation, pointing towards a potential link between rotational dynamics and the mechanism driving the event.

This paper addresses two primary areas: first, the rigorous theoretical examination of effective interpolation methods applicable to both effective quark-parton distributions (parton distribution functions) and quantum chromodynamics Lagrangians; second, the practical application of these interpolation techniques alongside numerical simulations to generate interpolated functions. These results establish highly precise starting points for subsequent global analyses, which determine the ultimate shape of parton distribution functions.

Sintering stands as a pivotal technique for enabling in situ 3D printing on the Moon and Mars. To optimize such operations, a comprehensive understanding of how to control the heat generated during sintering is essential. This research investigates the effects of varying sintering temperatures (200°C to 600°C) on the microstructure and mechanical properties—specifically compressive strength and elastic modulus—of simulated lunar and Martian regoliths that have been molded and subjected to sintering. Results indicate that exceeding a temperature of 200°C significantly alters the mechanical performance of these regolith types. Notably, Martian simulant exhibits distinct properties compared to lunar simant at high heat; specifically, it contains phyllosilicates that buffer thermal changes, yielding superior mechanical strength under extreme temperatures. Conversely, both samples show the development of a ceramic glass phase at temperatures above 200°C. This phase generates internal stresses that crack the ceramic matrix, thereby reducing overall strength. Furthermore, at temperatures exceeding 400°C, crystalline phases begin to form within the glass, which helps relieve internal stress and restore strength to the lunar simulant, while this strengthening mechanism is less pronounced or absent in the Martian variant. Additionally, both materials demonstrate that increasing particle size improves mechanical properties, yet the magnitude of this improvement and the optimal size parameter differ between lunar and Martian mixes. When a horizontal thread of liquid in air breaks up into droplets, surface tension drives this Rayleigh-Plateau instability. However, a similar effect occurs when a horizontal fibre pulling liquid air moves through water, causing a cylindrical liquid film to form rings if the thread is disturbed. This phenomenon is complicated by the presence of solid boundaries, where fluid behavior around the thread depends on whether the fluid slips along the surface or remains stuck. In our analysis, we focus on the scenario where liquid slides freely along both the thread and the boundary, a system we resolve using asymptotic methods to create a uniform approximation valid throughout space. Our theoretical predictions reveal that contact with a second solid body shifts the most perturbed mode of the thread and alters its period compared to an isolated thread, effects we validated through experiments on a horizontal fibre immersed in water. Furthermore, we demonstrate that allowing fluid slip significantly accelerates breakup, while also quantifying how the distance between liquid air and the boundary influences the resulting cycle period.

Diffusion models have recently emerged as potent frameworks for generating data across diverse domains, distinguishing themselves by mastering complex probability distributions through the meticulous reversal of noisy degradation processes. However, their deployment is hindered by sluggish training velocities. In response, this study introduces Multi-Stage Noised Training (MSNT), an enhanced strategy designed to accelerate training while maintaining fidelity to training. The proposed methodology is grounded in the hypothesis that ceising noise learning once signal components are fully reconstructed allows for performance enhancements. To validate this, MSNT introduces an initial phase dedicated to comprehensively acquiring noise evolution patterns and a secondary phase focusing exclusively on distribution alignment. These stages operate through three distinct training protocols tailored to the specific demands multi-phase learning. Experimental results demonstrate not only the empirical confirmation of our hypothesis but also the substantial improvement in training efficiency, with speedups reaching proportions as high as 4.64 compared to standard models.

Recognizing handwritten mathematical expressions is crucial for digitizing historical archives of math papers, an existing solution which involves experts annotating an image to produce a corresponding expression. This study investigates whether feature-rich image representations can enable a similar automatic recognition process for handwritten math equations, specifically exploring if these features allow a system to accurately interpret the math drawn, rather than just having experts map images to specific textual expressions.

This paper presents a straightforward strategy for generating synthetic speech durations. The core objective is to minimize the duration distribution mismatch between the training set and the speaker by creating a duration distribution that aligns closely with that of the target speaker. Our method leverages the median speech duration as a stable reference for each target speaker. The proposed approach offers two main advantages: it does not require retraining the system for each new speaker, and it demonstrates superior performance compared to using average speech duration instead.

Spatial occupancy models have gained significant traction in ecological research recently due to rising interest in how spatial processes influence species detection probabilities and abundance estimates. To facilitate this approach, the **spOccupancy** package in R offers an accessible interface for fitting single-species, multi-species, and integrated spatial occupancy models. Accounting for deviations in residual distributions, such as zero-inflation or non-Gaussian trends, allows researchers to address diverse ecological inquiries using limited data on presence/absence and count information. The package provides three primary interfaces to accommodate varying data structures: "matrix" for simple datasets, "sf" for complex, spatially explicit scenarios utilizing spatial vectors, and "matRn" designed specifically for massive matrices. This technical report presents "spOccupancy" with practical illustrations drawn from real-world ecological data to demonstrate its capabilities.

Dermatoscopy facilitates the visual diagnosis of skin conditions by revealing microscopic structures often invisible to the naked eye. Although dermatologists often diagnose these cases, diagnostic uncertainty is common, particularly for atypical lesions that may require a biopsy for confirmation. To help reduce the frequency of unnecessary procedures, we introduce the Skincare initiative, a dedicated AI framework for analyzing dermatoscopic images. This project leverages state-of-the-art deep learning to differentiate between benign and malignant cases while specifically identifying cancer types. The Skincare initiative offers a unique multimodal experience: dermatologists can interact directly with the model by uploading images, and the system responds by identifying the lesion and illustrating its detected features.

This study introduces a stochastic autoencoder framework designed to analyze non-linear trends and deviations in a dataset of 4,000 empirical spectra derived from 14 Type Ia supernovae. These spectra, obtained by the Supernova Ia Factory (SNIAF) consortium, were collected over a decade and represent the most extensive and varied collection of empirical Type Ia supernova spectral data to date. Each spectrum features 300 wavelength bands, with observations at an average of 10 days per spectrum, resulting in data that is both deep and wide. We implement two two-layered two-way stochastic autoencoders to extract non-linear features and detect anomalies. Initially, a model using 10 units identifies common spectral evolution patterns, while a model using five units captures unique, individual characteristics. Analysis of the latent space from the 10-unit model reveals a clear $\lambda$-shaped curve, with spectra at extreme wavelengths showing higher variance likely caused by stellar mass variations, though this effect diminishes toward central wavelengths due to lower variance. Finally, applying outlier detection to the 55-unit model successfully identifies distinct spectral anomalies, including Na I D lines, [O I] emission lines, and [Ca II] emission lines, with the latter appearing more frequently at earlier (bluer) phases.

This study examines the turbulent free plume generated by a turbulent, buoyant jet emerging from a circular source. The flow is stabilized through the injection of finite-sized inert, spherical particles that match the density of the surrounding ambient fluid. Through direct numerical simulations, we analyze the evolving three-dimensional velocity and temperature fields alongside particle trajectories, focusing on regimes where the particle Stokes number is approximately 0.15 and the Archimedes number is approximately 400. We determine that nearly all particles remain within the plume for durations exceeding the local large-eddy turnover time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that prolonged trajectory confinement results in a statistically significant increase in the time-averaged mean squared displacement of particles as they age. This finding confirms extensive plumeros mixing, during which the mean flow and individual trajectories exhibit approximately a 30% wider spread compared to a corresponding passive scalar distribution. These results provide robust support for practical models, such as the vorticity-buoyancy model, which assume high-plume residence for inert particles.

The behavior of epidemics is often modeled using the SIR (susceptible-infected-recovered) framework, a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) rooted in mean-field theory. This classical approach, however, degrades in quality as population segmentation—structuring groups based on shared geographic or social contexts—intensifies. Recently, spectral graph theory has provided a foundation for analyzing SIR dynamics on simple networks, establishing a connection between the extinction of infections and eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix. In this paper, we generalize these findings to hypergraphs, which capture complex, multi-way interactions. By extending established results, we derive both upper and lower bounds for the extinction time. Our results demonstrate that the initial growth rate of an epidemic relies on the "two-step counting measure," whereas the long-term persistence of an outbreak depends entirely on the "one-step counting measure." These concepts are generalized through spectral graph theory and applied here using 2-walks, reflecting multi-way correlations. Consequently, we propose an $\ell_p$-norm formulation for $p\in[1,2]$ to quantify spread potential, offering an effective method for assessing risk based on multi-way social structures.

The recent discovery of magnetic materials that exhibit both magnetocrystalline anisotropy and the Rashba effect has sparked considerable interest in the field. Specifically, the magnetic CrI₃ monolayer crystallizes in a hexagonal structure and operates as a c-axis ferromagnet with strong anisotropy. In contrast, its bulk counterpart, CrI₃, adopts a rhombohedral structure. Within monolayer CrI₃, the magnetic moments are localized on chromium atoms and align along the vertical axis. Consequently, stacking two such monolayers to create a bilayer results in a two-dimensional material with central symmetry, where the ferromagnetic alignment remains perpendicular. This convergence of properties—perpendicular ferromagnetism, strong anisotropy, and centrosymmetry—makes the CrI₃ bilayer a prime candidate for investigating magnetoelectric interactions. In this study, we present a theoretical analysis of the spin profile within such a configuration. Our findings reveal that a bilayer with parallel ferromagnetic alignment mimics the behavior of a magnetic insulator with Rashba-type anisotropy. Conversely, an anti-parallel arrangement resembles that of a 2D ferromagnetic insulator lacking such anisotropy. These spin configurations can be empirically verified using muon spin rotation techniques.

Although magnetic activity in solar-type stars is driven by mechanisms similar to the Sun's, the magnitude of differential rotation in these stars is significantly lower, particularly as they age. Even within Sun-like stars, differential rotation is not uniform throughout the entire convection zone; in the tachocline beneath it, a subsurface layer of stable stratification causes a sharp drop in shear, creating an anti-solar profile. Even if classical tachoclinal dynamics are excluded, the interplay between the stable zone and the overlying convection zone can still generate magnetic flux. Alternatively, dynamo processes may occur within the convection zone itself, where the rotational shear peaks, albeit at weaker intensities. Theoretical models indicate that this regional variation in differential rotation could significantly alter the resulting large-scale magnetic fields. To explore the implications of these factors, we developed 3D global magnetohydrodynamical simulations for a 1.2 solar-mass star, varying the depth of the convection zone while keeping the star's total mass constant. The study investigates how the location of the convection zone boundary and the outer differential rotation gradient affect magnetic cycles in systems with zones of reduced mixing. The findings reveal that narrower convection zones produce stronger magnetic cycles, a result that aligns with observed correlations between cycle strength and stellar mass. Additionally, the magnetic fields of 1.2 solar-mass stars are estimated to reach approximately 1 kilogauss.

To address common issues in existing multimodal architectures, this paper introduces a novel Universal K-Fan framework (UKF-DFSR). The system utilizes canonical canonical decomposition to generate unique, structure-specific feature sub-sets for each modality, while its "K-fan" design ensures universal compatibility across diverse applications. Consequently, redundant information is significantly minimized, reducing the required latency and enhancing model efficiency. To further strengthen generalization, the framework incorporates a component for sharing representations among multiple tasks. Based on these principles, the paper presents the K-fan fan-specific loss function, an objective function that has been proven both convex and consistent. Universal compatibility is demonstrated through evaluations across nine datasets spanning six distinct task categories, with the new architecture consistently outperforming four established canonical multimodal baselines across all experiments. Model checking serves as a critical technique for identifying bugs in software, yet standard approaches typically evaluate threads individually, which causes them to overlook concurrency errors. Various solutions have emerged to address this limitation by attempting to detect all interleavings that may arise during execution. Among these, Dynamic Partial Order Reduction (DPOR) stands out as a leading solution known for being complete and efficient. This paper introduces **McMini**, a model checker that extends the original Mini model used for educational purposes by incorporating basic MC4M features. Initially developed to teach fundamental concepts within both model checking and DPOR, McMini leverages these capabilities to identify bugs in multithreaded implementations.

The proliferation of fake and unverified information on social media platforms has posed significant challenges, particularly endangering public health during crises like the COVID-19 pandemic, prompting researchers to investigate the issue. This study centers on the popular messaging app WhatsApp, which has over 2 billion users worldwide, finding that more than half of its participants received alerts about misleading content. Previously, users could forward messages unlimited times, a capability recently capped at five shares per link to combat the spread of rumors. Our research examines whether this message forwarding restriction is effective in curting the dissemination of fake information. Through a series of controlled lab experiments, we assessed forward behaviors among participants who were either informed about or uninformed about the existence of misinformation. The findings indicate that informing users about misinformation leads to reduced forwarding of those specific messages, regardless of whether they have prior knowledge of such falsehoods beyond the explicit notification. Additionally, messages deemed as misinformation were forwarded fewer times compared to those considered neutral or beneficial by readers. Thus, we conclude that implementing limits on message forwarding can effectively hinder the online propagation of misinformation.

We establish estimates for the frequency spectrum of alleles within a branching population featuring generalized binary allele dynamics and featuring a supercritical average progeny generating function. Our findings demonstrate that, conditionally on non-extinction events, low allele frequencies follow a linear distribution pattern whereas high frequencies adhere to a step-like curve. Furthermore, as our approach converges toward an increasingly supercritical criticality threshold toward its limits, we derive the corresponding extinct allele frequency spectrum which exhibits logarithmic behavior. Finally, upon addressing simultaneous limits involving both time evolution and generation rates relative to each other, our framework yields a complete allelic frequency spectrum applicable to scenarios where extinction probabilities vanish in absolute terms.

While previous end-to-end approaches show promise, they are constrained by using only paired training data consisting of specific attack types and genuine speech. This limitation hinders models from generalizing to undetected attacks. To address this, we introduce the Vigilant Activation Function designed for deep neural networks, extending the concepts of K-means clustering and competitive learning. This function offers greater flexibility by working with unpaired, unbalanced datasets and through an unsupervised training process. "Extending the inflationary gravitational potential to a superspace framework naturally yields a supersymmetric multiplet. Consequently, efficient scalar field theories of inflation emerge as the component fields of this new supermultiplet, specifically as multiplets containing superior scalar components. Furthermore, we explore both abelian and non-abelian constructions of efficient supersymmetric field theories of inflation, successfully establishing local supersymmetry at large scales and efficient supersymmetric theories."

Photonic entanglement stands as a central achievement in the field of quantum information. While standard experiments generate photon pairs via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) and establish entanglement by selecting specific outcomes, this process produces an overall state of equal superposition that exhibits symmetry regarding the choice of basis. This work demonstrates a method to break such symmetry by filtering one of the outgoing beams through single-mode optical fibers, thereby creating an asymmetrical state of mixedness between the two parties. We verify this asymmetry experimentally by observing differences in entanglement and fidelity metrics on the optical levels, with the resulting effects further analyzed through polarization density matrices.

This work explores the interaction of surface electromagnetic resonances in microwave planar resonators with nanoscale light-matter excitations. We theoretically and numerically identify that terahertz emission from defects within resonators can be significantly amplified by this interaction, with amplification factors reaching up to three orders of magnitude when defect dimensions measure approximately 100 nm. We further establish that such sub-wavelength spatial enhancement persists well beyond the diffraction limit of light, lasting for distances exceeding one wavecycle, thereby enabling the operation of novel active and passive Terahertz technologies.

Financial markets are inherently complex, nonlinear, and difficult to unravel. As a result, many researchers lean toward simulating market dynamics using advanced agent-based models. This paper examines whether introducing new trading tactics within such models genuinely adds value or merely mimics existing strategies to harvest their historical performance. We achieve this by running two distinct simulations: a baseline model validated against real performance before the addition of a new trading strategy, and a comparative free-agent model allowing strategies to evolve without constraints. By contrasting the profits and risk metrics from the free-agent simulation with real-world outcomes, we determine if a strategy generates real economic value beyond replicating known successful approaches.

The author introduces the Stinger framework, an open-source solution for detecting and monitoring network attacks, noting its significant utility in securing industrial control and operational technology environments. Although dynamic protocol identification serves as a core component of Stinger, the paper details three specific attack vectors that compromise this mechanism: protocol parameter manipulation, denial of service via fake packets, packet structure abuse.

**Parabolic semiconductors and BCS superconductors interfaced on an atomic scale facilitate a unique quantum effect: effective gating of superconducting magnons via magnon gate fields. By applying a magnon gate field, the surface states of a two-dimensional semiconductor can be tuned, thereby controlling the density of magnons in a superconducting region adjacent to it. This phenomenon demonstrates the potential for effective magnon magnon gate fields in future quantum information processing applications involving superconducting circuits.**

Zero-shot learning addresses scenarios where a model is trained on a set of known classes and must later identify novel categories it has never encountered during training by leveraging descriptions shared between the novel and known categories. This technique is especially valuable in data-sparse environments involving sparse label annotations. This paper proposes a new zero-shot learning framework for data-centric tasks involving audio, leveraging the characteristics that both existing and new classes often appear together in specific contexts. The model is enhanced using zero-shot training with augmented contexts to capture these correlations more effectively. Experiments conducted on the YAO dataset, which focuses on bird song classification, and the Birdsong dataset, which involves acoustic identification, have validated these advantages.

This paper introduces an advanced proposal for verifying comprehensive entangments in high-dimensional GHZ states, extending previous protocols for both binary multiqubit entangments and those limited to pairs of levels. The category is determined by the relative performance gap between RGB and RGB-D versions. The resulting network processes each category separately, allowing the final output to be generated by selecting from either an RGB-specific or an RGB-D-specific branch. The proposed approach has been rigorously benchmarked against both real-world datasets and challenging synthetic datasets, and it has been verified to significantly surpass existing state-of-the-art models on both fronts.

This paper details our winning approach for the Identifying Aggressive Tweets task at SemEval-2019 Challenge 6. We adapted two established BERT fine-tuning strategies to generate predictions for aggressive language detection. We fine-tuned a BERT base model using both the entire training dataset to produce an ensemble of two classifiers, and a second, pre-trained BERT on an extended agglession-vocabulary to yield individual model predictions. We assess the contributions of these models by comparing their results from an all-agglssion-pre-training vs. the no-pre-training scenario. We complement BERT outputs with additional features to produce the final aggressive detection judgment. Our method achieved an F-1 score of 80.00, surpassing the public baseline of 76.00 and the submitted baseline of 78.80.

Multislice detector Computed Tomography (mSD-CT), which employs energy-resolved X-rays, offers a pathway to enhance CT imaging quality and accelerate acquisitions by simultaneously addressing artifact correction, denoising, and speed enhancements. This paper introduces a comprehensive variational framework designed for the reconstruction of polyenergetic CT data. The proposed 0-norm constrained convex optimization problem integrates a data fidelity term to handle Poisson noise with three regularization terms: one promoting total variation, another enforcing sparsity in the Fourier domain, and a third encouraging sparsity according to the Mixue-Beer law. Although the initial formulation is non-convex due to the Mixue-Beer law regularization, a convex reformulation is achieved through the introduction of auxiliary variables. To solve the resulting equivalent problem, we develop an efficient algorithm based on the augmented Lagrangian method. Experimental results on both simulated datasets and clinical mSD-CT scans demonstrate the system's superior performance in simultaneously achieving high-quality reconstruction, effective noise suppression, and accurate material decomposition.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) is a highly valuable application with numerous practical uses. As a substantial and ongoing challenge within Natural Language Processing and Vision, significant research has been dedicated to it. A primary obstacle in this field is language diversity; creating large, high-quality datasets annotated with correct character and word boundaries is difficult, particularly for low-resource languages. Consequently, these languages often suffer from underperformance compared to high-resource alternatives due to a scarcity of training data. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel data augmentation technique designed to improve low-resource HTR models by enhancing character composition. Evaluated on a multilingual dataset of handwritten receipts containing content in both high- and low-resource languages, our approach demonstrates significant improvements across all conditions, yielding an increase of up to 3.30 gars in character error rate reduction for the low-resource language evaluation.

Accomplishing first-principles calculations on atoms with high nuclear charge remains a major hurdle in theoretical and computational physics. This study introduces a novel method for simulating ground and excited states of such heavy atoms by merging two established techniques: Dirac-Fock variational calculations and Coupled Cluster with many-body expansion methods. To handle atoms containing thousands of electrons, we developed a scalable algorithm for generating correlation-consistent basis sets that are optimized for neutral atoms and adjusted for various ionization states. Applying our unified approach to carbon, we computed the binding energy of the $He$-$^{12}$Be$-$$\gamma$ triple-coincidence system, yielding values of 58.0(3) eV for its electronic structure.

Topological quantum states represent a promising avenue for housing robustly protected quantum information, with concepts like Chern numbers and Hopf indices serving as defining characteristics. This study employs two-dimensional visualizations and dynamic simulations to clarify the mechanisms underlying these topological features using the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model as a pedagogical entry point. By examining phenomena such as chiral symmetry, Peierls gaps, edge states, flux-induced state transitions, anti-cherial symmetry, and chiral states, this work facilitates a deeper grasp of these concepts and their significance within broader quantum frameworks where indices like Chern or Hopf are applied. Ultimately, this research facilitates discourse and instruction, demonstrating how computational exploration can substantiate and illuminate abstract theoretical principles in quantum physics.

This paper investigates when holomorphic compact composition operators exist on the Bergman space of an arbitrary bounded convex domain within $\mathbb{C}^n$. The author demonstrates that such an operator is compact if and only if the associated pullback transformation on the same domain is a finite rank operator. Additionally, the study extends these results to composition operators derived from holomorphic retracts and projections onto specific subdomains of $\mathcal{D}$, as well as composition operators associated with holomorphic maps terminating at an strongly pseudo-convexex domain $\mathcal{D}'$ across an extensive class of test domains characterized by an extensive set of properties.

We derive a dual description of type IIB superstring theory on the background AdS$_5\times$S$^5$, where the description preserves only $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetry as opposed to the standard $\mathcal{N}=4$ and arises via deformation of the parent model. This new framework retains a duality with a deformed five-dimensional IIB CFT characterized by $\mathcal{N}=1$ supersymmetry. Consequences of this finding extend beyond this specific case, potentially allowing the study of deformed CFTs through appropriate extensions and deformations of existing $\mathcal{N}=4$ duals. The foundational approach exploits the AdS/CFT correspondence itself: specific modifications to the bulk field theory are traced back to well-defined changes in the boundary CFT.

Object-oriented programming is widely adopted for developing applications that run effectively on GPUs; however, GPUs utilizing these languages often lack the necessary runtime memory allocators. Existing solutions either do not support object-oriented features or fail to optimize memory performance, resulting in inefficient usage and low throughput. To address these issues, we present DynaSOAr, a concurrent runtime memory allocator designed specifically for object-oriented GPU development and grounded in our Alpha-oriented Active Re-reference algorithm. DynaSOAr provides dynamic heap-based allocation while retaining the core advantages of our Underlying reference counting scheme. As a free-memory allocator, it introduces additional features such as dynamic growth capabilities. Evaluations demonstrate that DynaSOAr achieves superior dynamic allocation performance compared to the current state-of-the-art GPU allocator, CUDA. Furthermore, when benchmarked against a prior reference-based implementation of the virtual garbage collector, DynaSOAr delivers comparable overall system performance while significantly reducing the overhead specific to memory allocation.

We examine eight proposed $U(1)_X$ models, each being a subgroup influenced by $U(1)_X$ derived within the framework of the $\mathbf{16}$ representation of $SO(10)$. Detailed tables outlining the gauge couplings of these models are provided, revealing relationships with other standard $U(1)$ models encountered in gauge unification and grand unified theory literature. Furthermore, we analyze specific matter fields suitable for compacton construction within these frameworks. Our investigation demonstrates that the standard model gauge bosons constitute the most significant fields available for building compactons in these $U(1)_X$ models.
